claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements increases lattice distortion in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Greater lattice distortion raises hardness relative to alloys with minimized atomic size mismatch.
Greater lattice distortion raises yield strength relative to alloys with minimized atomic size mismatch.
Lattice distortion caused by atomic size mismatch impedes dislocation glide.
Two alloy series can have identical chemical compositions while differing in atomic size mismatch among their constituent elements.
Atomic-size-induced lattice distortions create heterogeneous local barriers to dislocation motion.
Atomic-size-induced lattice distortion raises the activation energy for dislocation motion.
The resulting impediment to dislocation glide increases resistance to plastic deformation.
The high-lattice-distortion series will have higher hardness than the low-lattice-distortion baseline under identical testing conditions.
The high-lattice-distortion series will have higher yield strength than the low-lattice-distortion baseline under identical testing conditions.
The low-size-mismatch baseline has lower lattice distortion and lower resistance to dislocation movement.
The proposed relationship applies primarily to single-phase, dislocation-dominated high-entropy alloys at ambient or moderate temperatures.
Recovery and other dynamic processes at elevated temperatures can mask lattice-distortion strengthening.
Significant local chemical order can dominate or confound strengthening attributed to lattice distortion.
Second-phase precipitates can dominate strengthening and make the lattice-distortion effect less pronounced.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase, or observation of similar glide barriers in both series, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis proposes changing atomic size mismatch among constituent elements, but the intervention and falsification design require identical compositions. Constituent atomic-size mismatch is ordinarily fixed by elemental identities and concentrations, so it cannot be independently varied at identical composition without introducing another variable such as chemical ordering, which the design says should be controlled.
